title: Software process
note: Modern teams ship in small increments and get feedback fast. Agile values working software and responding to change; continuous integration merges and tests changes many times a day; semantic versioning tells users what an upgrade will break. Technical debt is the future cost of shortcuts taken now.

read.title: Small batches, fast feedback
text: In 2001 seventeen developers met in Utah and wrote the Agile Manifesto. Its four values favor individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration, and responding to change over the things that had dominated big projects: processes and tools, comprehensive documentation, contract negotiation, and following a plan. The idea was not that documents and plans are worthless, but that delivering working software in small pieces and learning from it beats predicting everything up front.

Continuous integration applies the same thinking to code. Developers merge into the main line at least daily, and every merge triggers an automated build and test run, so integration problems surface within minutes instead of at the end of a release. Continuous delivery keeps the main line always releasable; continuous deployment goes further and ships every passing change automatically.

Semantic versioning makes releases legible to the people who depend on them. Breaking the public API bumps the major version, adding backward-compatible features bumps the minor version, and backward-compatible fixes bump the patch. Shortcuts taken to ship sooner are fine if chosen deliberately, but, as Ward Cunningham warned with his debt metaphor, they charge interest on every later change until someone pays them down.

o: They matter, but less than working software and adapting
